pedagogy.summary: Calculating simple probability is the procedural skill of applying P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes to equally-likely situations and giving the answer as a fraction in simplest form. The work is fluent, accurate execution across contexts (dice, bags, spinners): counting the favourable outcomes, counting the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), forming the fraction, checking the outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying.
bestPractices: Rehearse the same three-step routine across varied contexts — count favourable, count total, write and simplify — so it transfers beyond dice
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes (favourable included), heading off the part-part error
Require a check that outcomes are equally likely BEFORE applying the formula
Connect 'more favourable outcomes → larger probability' by varying a bag's composition and watching the fraction grow
Always express in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale
keyRepresentations: P(event) = favourable/total written under the situation
Bags, dice, spinners with countable equally-likely outcomes
Part-whole diagram of the outcome set
commonMisconceptions: Writing favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 rather than 3/10 for 3 blue among 10
Applying the formula to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely (an uneven spinner, a weighted die)
Failing to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly
Miscounting the total — forgetting to include the favourable outcomes in the denominator

learn.summary: Learners build fluency with P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally-likely situations, giving answers as fractions in simplest form. The core routine is: check the outcomes are equally likely, count favourable outcomes, count the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), form the fraction, and simplify. Practice should span varied contexts (dice, bags, spinners) and target the part-part error (favourable-to-unfavourable) and the misapplication of the formula to unequal outcomes.

activities.title: Varied probability ladder with simplest form
feedback: If a learner writes 3/7 for the bag, recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes: everything that could be drawn is 10, so 10 goes on the bottom, giving 3/10.

If a learner applies the formula to an uneven spinner, prompt the equally-likely check first: when sections are different sizes the colour counts are not counts of equally-likely outcomes, so the simple formula does not apply.

If a learner leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly, scaffold the simplifying step and confirm 1/4 sits at the same point on the 0-to-1 scale \u2014 simplifying does not change the actual chance.
If a learner combines numbers arbitrarily with no favourable-over-total structure, return to counting favourable, then total, then writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: The objective is fluent, accurate execution of favourable/total across contexts with simplest-form answers. Varied contexts support transfer beyond dice, and items built from the exact errors (part-part, unsimplified, formula on an uneven spinner) make the common mistakes surface and get corrected.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.

Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Work a short series of problems, each a probability to be formed and then simplified: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles \u2014 find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die \u2014 find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold \u2014 find P(gold).
For each item, first confirm the outcomes are equally likely, then count the favourable outcomes, then count the WHOLE set of possible outcomes (including the favourable ones) for the denominator.
Write each probability as a fraction and simplify where possible (e.g. 2/8 \u2192 1/4).
On the bag item, if you write 3/7, stop and recount: the denominator is all 10 marbles, including the 3 blue ones, so the answer is 3/10.
Encounter at least one unequal-outcome situation (e.g. an uneven spinner with different-sized sections) and decide whether the simple formula applies before using it.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the whole set of equally-likely outcomes, favourable included \u2014 so P(blue) among 3 blue and 7 red is 3/10, not 3/7. The simple favourable/total formula only applies when outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying (2/8 = 1/4) names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.

activities.title: Editable bag: watch the fraction form and simplify
feedback: If a learner expects only the numerator to matter, vary the non-favourable counts and show that the denominator (whole set) and the scale marker both respond \u2014 e.g. adding red marbles enlarges the total, so P(blue) falls (as long as the bag has at least one blue; with no blue it stays 0).
Confirm that the simplified fraction lands on the same point of the 0-to-1 line as the unsimplified one \u2014 the chance is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A live model that forms favourable/total as the child edits the bag, shows simplification, and marks the scale can reinforce WHY the denominator is the whole set and how composition drives the value. This may support conceptual understanding alongside the procedural fluency. The interactive updating (live fraction, scale marker) is an optional illustrative mechanism, not required equipment.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.
learnerActions: Edit the composition of a bag (e.g. add or remove blue and red counters) and read the probability fraction as it forms.
Identify the WHOLE set as the denominator each time the bag changes, confirming favourable counters are part of that total.
Watch the simplified form of the fraction and a marker on a 0-to-1 line move as the composition changes.
Predict: 'If I add 5 more red marbles, which number in the fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?' then check against the live display.
activities.intendedInsight: More favourable outcomes relative to the whole set raise the probability; the denominator is always the whole outcome set. Seeing the fraction and its position on the scale update as the bag changes connects composition to the value of the probability.

activities.title: Worked example and Socratic 'out of how many?' check
feedback: If a learner gives odds (part-part, e.g. 3 to 7), re-pose 'and out of how many altogether?' until they name 10 as the whole set.
Confirm the worked fraction is in simplest form before moving on.
activities.rationale: A worked example plus targeted questioning models the routine and can surface the part-part misconception through explanation. This may build understanding but, on its own, does not supply the repeated varied practice that fluency needs \u2014 pair it with the practice ladder.
sourceClaims: Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Study a worked die or bag example: identify the favourable outcomes, then the whole set, then reveal the simplified fraction.
When asked 'and out of how many altogether?', state the full count of possible outcomes, not just the non-favourable ones.
Explain in your own words why the total includes the favourable outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the total as the whole set (favourable included) catches the part-part slip before it becomes a habit and makes the structure of the formula explicit.

constraints: Require an equally-likely check BEFORE applying favourable/total; the simple formula does not apply to uneven spinners, weighted dice, or other unequal-outcome situations.
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes, with favourable outcomes included \u2014 this heads off the part-part (favourable-to-unfavourable) error.
Always express answers in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.
A worked example with tap-to-reveal counts models the routine but cannot by itself provide the repeated, varied practice fluency requires; use it as an introduction alongside practice.

A single final answer does not reveal whether the learner counted the whole set, checked equal-likelihood, or simplified; favour formats that require constructing and simplifying the fraction across varied contexts.
The editable-bag live fraction, simplification display, and 0-to-1 scale marker are optional illustrative supports, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked values: P(blue) with 3 blue of 10 total = 3/10; P(4) on a fair six-sided die = 1/6; P(gold) with 2 of 8 equal sections = 2/8 = 1/4. These are internally consistent across the source fields.
The part-part value 3/7 (3 blue to 7 red) is intentionally retained only as an error to be corrected, never presented as a valid answer.

Source claims support the favourable/total principle and the need to teach against the part-part error; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format (quiz vs interactive vs dialogue). Any 'only a quiz drills this' or '3D adds nothing' framing has been reduced to scoped statements about observable affordances.

The legacy pedagogy summary listed the equally-likely check after forming the fraction, while its best-practice guidance placed the check before applying the formula; the corrected routine places the check first, consistent with the stated best practice.

probeDeeper: In 3/10, where does the 10 come from — is blue part of it?
You wrote P(gold) = 2/8. Can you write that more simply? Does simplifying change the actual chance?
If I added 5 more red marbles, which number in your fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?
Would this formula still work if the spinner's sections were different sizes? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: (a) P(blue) = 3/10 — three favourable out of ten counters altogether, blue included in the total; (b) P(4) = 1/6; (c) P(gold) = 2/8 = 1/4 simplified. The child forms favourable/TOTAL each time, puts the whole set in the denominator, and simplifies where possible.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 for 3 blue among 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes; the total is everything that could be drawn, so 10 not 7 goes on the bottom
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The denominator is the count of the OTHER outcomes rather than the whole set

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies favourable/total to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the equally-likely check first; if sections are unequal the colour counts are not counts of equally likely outcomes and the simple formula does not apply
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the formula straight onto an uneven spinner or weighted device without checking the sections/outcomes are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to simplify, or simplifies incorrectly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the simplifying step and confirm the simplified fraction sits at the same point on the scale; this is an execution lapse, not a conceptual gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly

responseLevels.gap: Cannot form the fraction or combines numbers arbitrarily; no favourable-over-total structure
responseLevels.full: Computes favourable/total across all three contexts with the whole set in the denominator, checks the outcomes are equally likely, and gives each answer in simplest form
responseLevels.partial: Forms favourable/total for the easy die case but writes part-part for the bag, forgets or botches simplifying, or applies the formula without checking equal-likelihood

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems on cards with paper: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles — find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die — find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold — find P(gold). Say: 'Work out each probability and write it as a fraction in its simplest form.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they count the TOTAL correctly, whether they check the outcomes are equally likely, and whether they simplify.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the denominator is the whole set (3/10) or the leftovers (3/7), whether they check equal-likelihood before applying the formula, and whether they simplify — none of which a single final answer would expose.
